svg.aria-label: Diagram: the two firewall log formats and how each is blind to the other's targeting metadata, with the legacy VPC format unable to record secure tags, FQDNs, threat intelligence lists and address groups while the policy format cannot record network tags or service accounts; the connection-based logging model with its ten-minute idle timer, one entry per allowed connection with reply traffic unlogged, and a denied connection repeating every five seconds per five-tuple; the per-machine-type connection logging caps measured over five-second intervals and the best-effort caveat that applies even below the cap; and the cost, where firewall logs are billed twice, carry no free allotment, and still incur the generation charge if you exclude them from Cloud Logging
svg.title: Firewall rules logging: two formats with opposite blind spots, a connection model that is not a packet model, and two charges
svg.text: There are two firewall log formats, and each cannot record what the other targets on.
Both log connections rather than packets, both are capped and best-effort, and both bill twice.
Two formats, opposite blind spots
The LEGACY VPC format cannot log the advanced Cloud NGFW metadata: secure tags, FQDNs,
threat intelligence lists, address groups, region codes. Ten named fields.
The POLICY format cannot log the legacy metadata: source_tag, target_tag,
source_service_account, target_service_accounts. #72’s entire subject.
Only policy logs record the INTERCEPTED disposition and APPLY_SECURITY_PROFILE_GROUP.
Only the legacy format may set the IP protocol field to ALL. Policy rules cannot.
A connection record is not a packet record
An entry is created when a connection is ESTABLISHED, not per packet. A connection stays
active while packets flow at least once every 10 MINUTES; each packet resets the timer.
ALLOW: logged ONCE for the whole duration. Reply traffic is stateful and is NOT logged.
DENY: every unique 5-tuple is logged, and REPEATS EVERY 5 SECONDS while packets arrive.
Turning logging on mid-flight logs nothing: an already-active connection is picked up only
after it has been idle 10 minutes. For continuous visibility use VPC Flow Logs instead.
The cap is per VM machine type, and it stops growing at 8 vCPUs
Limits are the most connections loggable in a FIVE-SECOND interval, per VM instance:
f1-micro 100 · g1-small 250 · 1 to 8 vCPUs 500 PER vCPU · above 8 vCPUs 4,000 flat.
So 500 x 8 = 4,000 is a ceiling, not a rate: a far larger machine logs no more than an
8-vCPU one. That is 800 connections per second, however big the VM gets.
And entries are BEST EFFORT: they can be dropped under heavy traffic BELOW the cap.
You are billed twice, and the free allotment does not apply
1. NETWORK TELEMETRY generation: $0.25 per GiB for the first 10,240 GiB, then tiered down
2. CLOUD LOGGING vended logs storage, billed separately from your other logs.
The 50 GiB per project per month free allotment is for ordinary logs. Vended network logs
have NO free allotment, so the first gibibyte of firewall logging is already chargeable.
Excluding them from Cloud Logging does not help: the telemetry charge still applies.
What it can never show you: anything that is not TCP or UDP; the implied rules; rules in
legacy networks; and the external IP of your own VM — the log carries the address the VM
sees on the packet header, as tcpdump would, so a public address never appears.
The lever worth pulling: records split into BASE and OPTIONAL METADATA fields, and you can
exclude the metadata to cut storage — losing exactly the fields #75 wanted for hygiene.
